report:
**Conclusion:** Your assessment is supported by the best available evidence: ivermectin has **not been shown to lower the risk of death from COVID-19**. It should not be used for COVID-19 treatment outside a clinical trial.

Early small studies and some meta-analyses suggested benefit, but many had serious limitations (small samples, bias, inconsistent methods, and later concerns about study integrity). Subsequent larger, better-controlled randomized trials have found no clinically meaningful benefit. For example, a large placebo-controlled trial of a relatively high ivermectin dose found no improvement in sustained recovery; its results do not support ivermectin for mild-to-moderate COVID-19. This trial was not primarily powered to establish a mortality benefit, but its negative results align with the broader evidence base.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36807465/

A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis that searched trials through June 2023 evaluated clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality; it does not establish a reliable mortality benefit.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38510038/

Major health authorities accordingly do not recommend it: WHO states the evidence is inconclusive and advises ivermectin for COVID-19 only in clinical trials, regardless of illness severity.  
https://www.who.int/news-room/feature-stories/detail/who-advises-that-ivermectin-only-be-used-to-treat-covid-19-within-clinical-trials

The FDA has neither authorized nor approved ivermectin to prevent or treat COVID-19, and warns that inappropriate use—especially veterinary products or excessive doses—can cause serious toxicity.  
https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/ivermectin-and-covid-19
